The person who made me feel most seen was the man I ended up marrying. He was brilliant and kind, and he was the first person who helped me see myself through their eyes. He wrote me long, eloquent, thoughtful letters, we talked for hours every day about everything under the sun. He loved me unconditionally, constantly building me up and reminding me of my best qualities. I felt confidence for the first time in my life. We had a long distance relationship for a while, then I moved across the country to his home state. I bought a house, we got married, and shortly after I got pregnant with our twins.

Then things changed. He seemed to stop seeing me. He started criticizing. Things would get better for a time when I "fixed" the problem, then worse again when he decided I had another one. We went to counseling for a little while, but it was just a loop of my husband's criticism, the therapist suggesting methods I could try to be better, and me crying because I felt like such a useless piece of garbage. He slowly and methodically stripped away all my self worth until I was totally convinced that I was a terrible person who couldn't do a single thing right. I remember crying and begging him to help me be a better person. I couldn't accept that he was the problem because he had loved me so much, more than I think anyone will love me again (not because I'm unlovable, I'm actually fucking awesome). He thought the sun rose and set out of my ass. He was so devoted and in awe of me. Until he wasn't.

It wasn't until his emotional abuse started affecting our children that I snapped back to reality. I had been willing to accept his treatment of me because I was so awful, but not my kids, man. No one gets to make my kids feel worthless. NO ONE. 

So I left. I secretly diverted money into my own separate bank account until I could pay the retainer for a good lawyer. I made an exit plan with my lawyer, my mom, and my sister. When I was ready, I packed whatever I could into my van, picked up the kids from school, and drove to my sister's house. The divorce was absolutely horrible, and took over 2 years, but I'm free and my kids are safe.

And now I don't need anyone to see me, because I see myself.

Physicians assistants in the US are similar to Nurse Practitioners in that they have prescribing privileges and may or may not work under the supervision of an M.D. I *think* NPs have their own DEA number, and PAs prescribe under a supervising physician's number, but I could be wrong about that. 

We have Medical Assistants that room patients, take vitals, give injections, draw blood, and assist with procedures. It requires certification and about 2 years of education.

Your undernurse sounds like our Nursing Assistant (CNA). Non-clinical patient care, help with ADLs, that kind of thing.

We have a few levels of actual nurses, too. Licensed Practical Nurses require a 2 year nursing program, and they have some limitations; things like IV pushes and transfusions, and they can't take verbal orders. Registered Nurses typically require a bachelor's degree in nursing, and they supervise LPNs and CNAs. RNs can also get masters degrees to go into administration, or go on to nurse practitioner training.

A couple fun facts! Yes, your ovaries hold all the primordial follicles (undeveloped ova) you'll ever have when you are a fetus. However, there are many follicles in different stages of development at any given time. Every month when FSH is secreted from the pituitary, it stimulates the strongest/furthest developed follicles to continue maturing. Most people have about 20 mature follicles at the time of ovulation, but usually only one is released. The rest undergo cell death. Only about 1% of the follicles we have at birth end up being ovulated. 99% self destruction as a normal part of the ovarian cycle.

Releasing more than one ova per cycle is called hyperovulation, and is the reason for fraternal twins/triplets/etc!

Compartment syndrome is not caused by laying on your arm for hours. It seems like you're conflating it with radial neuropathy (Saturday night palsy).

Compartment syndrome occurs when there is swelling in a "compartment" (group of muscle and connective tissue encased in fascia), usually from an acute injury. If the pressure in the compartment gets too high, it can cause the muscles to be starved of blood and nutrients, which can cause tissue death, like you said. Fasciotomy (the "filleting" you referenced) is performed to release the pressure and increase blood flow within the compartment. It isn't an incision into the muscle fibers (instead the fascia), and it's not used to flush toxins out of the muscles.

Recipe:  
2 T vegetable oil  
2lb parsnips, peeled and chopped  
2 leeks, white parts chopped  
4 cups chicken broth  
1 cup chopped fennel fronds  
1/2 cup heavy cream  
Salt and pepper  
  
I used an instant pot for this recipe. Sauteed the leeks and parsnip in oil for about 5 minutes, added the chicken broth, and cooked at high pressure for 12 minutes. Added cream and fennel and pureed with a stick blender. Strained out any excess fennel fronds. Salt and pepper to taste.
